title: The Final Station
text: Yet another let-down. A game I wanted to love(TM). I updated the review after finishing the game. The atmosphere is really thick and well done. Reminded me of Limbo and INSIDE in some way, and that's a compliment to a highest degree. The gameplay seems a bit bulky at first, but you'll get over it. I was sold the very first seconds. Sounds are well done, and so is the music. The train is a weird thing. It's kind of Diner Dash mini game where you have to make sure everyone is healthy and satisfied, and your train does not overload. The customers are talking something, but most of the time I'm missing it out as I'm dashing around. I'd love to read the discussion they're having from somewhere. But then you start to get to more combat intensive places. Rooms full of enemies, low on clips and getting mauled time after time. Death has no meaning in this game, so you keep on trying and trying. I gave up. There was a ladder, and room full of baddies. Could not get to the room without dying. Could not shoot enemies from the floor below. I HATE THOSE LADDERS. Also, cardboard boxes and other items seem to be much more effective than the pistol. Fair enough. Ended up carrying a toilet seat half the map just in case :P I'm not happy with the game. It just doesn't seem to have enough interesting gameplay to warrant the price or my time. All the places seem alike, and there is very little interesting things in there. Story is told via static scenery and post-it notes.. rather easy solution for game with designed levels. Makes me wish it was some roguelike/procedurally generated game (honestly I though it would be like that based on the trailer though they did not make any claims about it. It just felt like that). Feels like a missed opportunity. Unfortunately I cannot recommend the game in its current form (the usual I'd give it a "meh" but due to lack of it it's thumbs down). EDIT: Finally finished the game. Unfortunately it turned out to be quite bad. While progressing, the feeling of detachment became stronger and stronger. The story, which is actually quite hard to understand and badly written to be honest, does not have any build-up towards the ending. The ending was a huge disappointment. There was no focus on the protagonist, his motives, or background, leaving the ending quite cold and uninteresting. The game is full of beautiful vistas and thick atmosphere, but instead of cohesive whole it started to feel like I'm jumping from scenario to another without any actual drama, and more like just for the sake of showing different environments. Anyway. There's a real effort here, but unfortunately it doesn't not work. Not recommended unless you get it really cheap and have few hours to waste.

title: The Final Station
text: It's impossible to review this without spoilers, so if that's something you want to avoid: get it, it's good, go in blind if you can. . . . . Still with me? Okay. Final Station isn't what it bills itself to be. I picked it up expecting a train-based scavenging roguelike, and that's what it is for a little while, but only as a disguise. What it is is a heavily narrative game hiding inside the shell of a narrative-lite experience. There's a lot of visual storytelling going on here--which is good, because the translation still feels a bit shaky in places. Core gameplay works like this: you get on a train, play a distracting minigame to keep diesel fumes from flooding the passenger car while you eavesdrop on the conversations of your passengers, and occasionally bring them a snack or a medkit to keep them from dying. Every so often, you stop and scavenge a station for food, medkits, and crafting scraps. Zombies attack you when you do, and you spend a lot of time walking slowly backwards punching them in the belly. If you can get your passengers to a safe station further down the line, they give you money, gear, and crafting scraps. Then you pick up more and the cycle begins again...at least for a little while. The story of the game is told in the background, and it's a surprisingly haunting one. It's also, by design, unfinished. The plotlines don't resolve. You get left with some suspicions, and you can follow some trails of lore pretty far through the game, but ultimately it terminates in a Sopranos ending that doesn't clear up any part of what you've just played through. This is frustrating to someone who likes there to be a meaning in things, but the game ends the way life does, messy and unfinished, and I think that's probably the point. Ultimately, you won't regret getting to dip into the gameworld, and the train gameplay elements are fun, even if they ultimately get dropped. There's some absolutely wonderful level design, despite being perfectly linear, and the soundtrack knows how to move deftly between mellow and tense as the mood changes. This is well worth its price, and a steal on sale.

title: The Final Station
text: You know, I think is the kind of game where it's best to go in completely blind. No reviews, no pros and cons, no preconceived notions. Just dive in. The first few moments of the game are immediately gripping, and the introduction to the world you're going to be playing in is perfectly paced and intriguing. But hey, if you insist on at least SOME information before you buy a game then here you go: is a strange mixture of side-scrolling shooter, survival game, and a dash of management game. You're playing as the conductor of a small train during the alien apocalypse, carrying important cargo that could change the tide of the battle plus whatever survivors you find on the way. The gameplay alternates between the shoot-y exploring-y parts where you scrounge for supplies in the outside world, and the parts where you frantically run back and forth in the train trying to keep you bleeding passengers from dying and the various machinery from breaking down. The clever part of this, and the thing that ties the two gameplay sides together, is that your inventory is common for both. Meaning that the medkit you spend on yourself on the field is one less medkit you can use on your passengers, and vice versa. This leads to the necessity for strategy during exploration; do you spend bullets and health to get to the precious food and crafting supplies behind the enemy monsters? Do you quickly go to your objective and back, hoping the supplies you already have will be enough? Both of these options can leave you screwed if you're not careful. And it's exactly this caution that puts you in the mindset of a survivor. Because while this is by no means a horror game, there is a certain tension and dread following in your footsteps. I had gotten into the habit of instinctively backing up when opening doors, paranoid about enemies rushing me. I would decide to conserve my dwindling bullets, only to waste them in a panic when surrounded by too many monsters. I would feel disoriented and suspicious whenever I visited safe zones populated by actual normal human beings. The game is very effective in achieving emotional responses from you, and there were even some parts that were surprisingly and delightfully creepy that definitely left an impression on me. The story itself is left mysterious, with information mostly gained from the rumors and gossiping of your passengers, and from the remnants of various strange past events you encounter during your travels. The world-building is slow but clever, and the moments when the bigger picture starts becoming clearer are particularly memorable. All in all it's the general atmosphere created from its seperate parts that is the game's greatest strength, and it's enhanced by the beautiful pixel art in the backgrounds and level design. Sadly no game is without flaws, and I'll start with a more personal nitpick: I thought the game just wasn't... well, hard . There's some talk in the beginning about how maybe you can't keep all your passengers alive and should prioritize who to save, but honestly if you're a basically decent player and explore often you won't have that much trouble with it. Maybe I'm a masochist but when I play survival games sometimes I want a more hardcore challenge, especially on a second playthrough, and this isn't really an option here as you can't choose a difficulty level. There aren't even enough achievements to make any self-imposed challenges worth it. What you get is the same each time. I should also mention the playtime, which is a bit short, with the game lasting about 4-5 hours. I actually don't think this is a negative point on its own, since there was enough content for me to feel satisfied, and anything more would probably end up being too repetitive and tiring. The negative aspect is that there is barely any replayability to it. The game can be loosely devided in 3 parts (plus prologue and epilogue) so I expected at the very least a chapter select option when I finished, but nope. You gotta start from the very beginning. And since like I said there are no difficulty levels to choose, you have bascially no incentive to start again. So yes, this is a game meant to be played only once. However, in the end the strength of the experience you get is more than enough to make it feel worth playing. (I was certainly impressed enough with the game to write this way too long review to recommend it!) So if you like clever little atmospheric indie games that try to be something a bit more unique, then don't let the downsides deter you. Give this a try. It's worth it.

text: To begin, let me offer the disclaimer that I was a Kickstarter backer of this game. And boy, it sure does not disappoint. Either I've been very lucky in backing mostly successful projects, or I've got a well-honed sense for detecting , but this is one Kickstarter/SEA project that did exactly what it promised and that very nicely. So aside from the highly attractive and tasteful low-poly art direction and the superb soundtrack, the gameplay is highly enjoyable! You don't see that very often, sadly. It does this refreshing back-and-forth between scavenging gameplay (the player character on foot evading predators and grabbing loots) and rafting gameplay (steering the player character's raft down the river). I say refreshing not because it's some revolutionary new paradigm in game design, but because the two alternating gameplay modes refresh your energy and desire to keep playing. This War Of Mine does a similar kind of thing, and both games do a very addictive "one more turn" thing dangerously conducive to all-nighter play sessions. While the controls supposedly optimized for a gamepad (ideally an xbone from what I understand), the game handles just fine with Mouseboard and Key. Been playing it that way since alpha and no issues. Really, the only place where it might hit a snag is aiming that darn bow Scout (the player character) is able to craft in the mid/late game. Possibly it's easier with a stick, but I couldn't tell ya. Can't be any worse than whiffing 90% of shots trying to aim it with a mouse. However, there is currently a small discrepancy in the two control schemes in that the gamepad controls allow you to pan the camera and look ahead of where Scout is walking, while there does not appear to be such a binding or capability in the keyboard control scheme. What's up with that, devs? But I'm reasonably confident they'll get around to fixing that sooner or later. Right? Generally speaking the game, while not super difficult or mind-bogglingly complex (which is by no means to say it's "casual," far from it!), is a treat in all of the ways games can be. Visually, musically, in terms of refreshing and satisfying gameplay modes, and in terms of high replayability, TFITF will not disappoint! Highly recommended for any fan of Rogue-like games, low poly art, and lovely folksy music and atmosphere.

title: The Flame in the Flood
text: I generally like 3rd Person survival games. I love Project Zomboid. I like Don't Starve. I appreciate what This War of Mine is trying to do. I couldn't get by the look of NEO Scavenger. But regardless of whether I like them or not, one this is true: I suck at them. I never win. I rarely get into a stable position. While some people are living for years in PZ, I'm dead in 5 days. While some folks can build a massive base on Don't Starve, I think I've made it to winter once...with mods to make it easier. I had to mod This War of Mine to get through it. So I finally picked up Fame in the Flood during the Steam sale. I waited until a good sale because it was likely that I'd get only a couple hours in it given that it wasn't moddable and I'm terrible at such games. I was wrong. While flawed, this is a greatly entertaining game. First of all I find the setting charming. As a former whitewater guide, I love floating down rivers. It's unique and beautiful. Add in some great - perfect for this setting - music and you wind up with a great atmosphere. The graphics are functional but I'm not as big a fan of the art style. It didn't put me off though. The game is best played through an XBox controller rather than keyboard and mouse (but both are functional). As for the gameplay, this is a flawed but ultimately satisfying game. The core gameplay is your character is floating down a river and pulling off at various stops. You gather, craft and push back off to float down the wild river some more to make progress. In your way aren't zombies or weird monsters. The dangers here are more mundane but still terrifying - hunger, thirst, wolves, disease, sickness, exposure and so forth. The challenge in the game is scarcity (which is typical of this type of game). You're rarely going to have enough stuff to do everything you want and you're going to have to prioritize. FitF doesn't give you much backpack space and so you're always going to struggle to figure out what to carry. You're going to have to leave stuff behind that is useful. You're going to make food, water, clothing, traps, bandages, herbal remidies, raft upgrades and so forth to overcome the dangers of this world. Note there's no real combat here. While you can make a bow to hunt with a bit and traps to catch food or defend yourself, this isn't a combat game. You're always playing defensively and you're not going to craft a sword to slay wolves with. If you're looking for a combat oriented game, this isn't it. In fact, this has less combat than any survival game I can think of but I think that's a strength and not a weakness. So what are the flaws? Well, inventory management is supposed to be part of the challenge but frankly it's one of the more annoying aspects of the game. You're going to be in your inventory A LOT and the UI is fine but it's still really annoying. You're going to spend a lot of time in that inventory screen. There's also no modding support for this game which is unheard of in this genre. Thus this is a WYSIWYG (look it up) game - it is what it is and you're not getting anything else. While some would say that means the game is unfinished, I don't think so. I've encountered no bugs and no crashes in 10 hours of play, so I see this game as finished. And to come back full circle to the opening paragraph, it's also winnable - at least for me on easy mode. It took a few tries but on easy I was able to progress (with liberal use of reloading) all the way to the end. So if these games are typically too difficult, this one isn't. And if you're good at these games, there are other difficulty levels which I'm sure can provide an ample challenge. In conclusion, this is a charming, well-constructed and entergaining game that deserves your patronage if you like this genre. It won't go down as a classic but you'll likely have some very fond memories of this title long after you move on to something else. As for me, I'm getting ready to get back on the river. title: The Flame in the Flood
text: Rogue-lite Survival Craft-'Em-Up with much joyous rafting but nowhere to go. ----- The Flame in the Flood has a brilliant soundtrack and some cool rafting sections. Unfortunately, for me, the whole thing was a bit shallow. You will exhaust all your crafting options within about an hour's worth of play and then it's just a case of keepin' on raftin'. Aside from the new locations and occasionally a new beasty to contend with, there is very little to keep you interested in the game as it progresses from a mechanical standpoint. The crafting itself feels similarly shallow. You can cook food, gather and purify water, make medical supplies, clothes, tools and traps, which might sound like a lot, but there is nothing that stands out as being particularly interesting to do. It feels like they went strongly for the "Man vs Nature" angle but failed to make nature scary, and the music and the aesthetics being kind of cute and relaxing also saps any sense of urgency or threat you might experience. I think I would like to raft down a river stopping off at random points for supplies in real life some day, but maybe this game just wasn't for me.

text: I recommend this excellent little game, while warning readers that it has rather limited replayability. Even though it has an Endless mode that is procedurally generated, the game is far too easy once you know what you are doing. This is compounded by a further very major problem: After a large amount of miles travelled (100+) in Endless mode, the game then applies "artificial difficulty" in that it simply stops spawning Repair Stations for you to get your raft fixed at. This means that every single endless run will simply (and predictably) end with you drowning as your raft health is chipped away by river hazards until it is ultimately destroyed. Furthermore I would warm impatient players away. Sometimes this game will simply decide to kill you on a whim. Whether it simply decides not to spawn any flint for the first 10 miles - meaning you cannot make the basic knife, meaning you cannot craft anything else at all, meaning you will starve - or whether it just decides to spawn 3 wolves at every single stop you make when you are desperate for food or sleep. You are basically at the mercy of RNG. You should expect to have to restart a good 3 to 4 times for every 'decent' run you make, no matter how experienced you are with the game. I've also had all my progress wiped by a bug that corrupted my save a couple of times. However, those few decent runs you do manage are sheer bliss and tremendous fun. So...recommended, but with hesitation.

title: The Flame in the Flood
text: This game is lacking so much quality control, it's not even funny. Most notably, you can't change the keybindings, and the default key for inventory is "i", so have fun hitting that with your left hand in a pinch. The game has a checkpoint system, but if you have a status effect that will kill you without the right treatment and you literally cannot find the item to save you, there's no freaking point. That's bloody terrible design. While crafting the game isn't paused, so hostile animals can spawn while you're making stuff. And there's a 24/7 windstorm with a million leaves crossing the screen every minute, while you're staring at the bloody inventory screen, and even when there are absolutely no trees upwind of you. So much about this game is ridiculously obnoxious, it's like the devs just gave up on trying to polish The Flame in the Flood. Two years ago key rebinding was on a dev's to-do list, and that was completely abandoned. Just watch someone else play this game on YouTube. This is probably one of the worst $15 purchases you can make on Steam.

title: The Journey Down: Chapter One
text: The Journey Down: Chapter One is a fantastic, but short, PnC (point & click) adventure game.  The game's content is very similar to Grim Fandango.  While the graphics are cartoonish and flamboyant, the humor and overall vibe is directed towards an adult audience.  The gameplay is not like Grim Fandango, but rather the style of the old school Monkey Island series.  Manipulating inventory is easy, as you just drag an item over to another item, whether it be on the screen or in the inventory.  There aren't any complex inventory combinations, and the puzzles are very intuitive.  The one thing that bothered me about the game is they sometimes drop hints when you are attempting to solve a puzzle.  This might be nice for games where the puzzles are less intuitive, but the puzzles in this game really aren't that hard to begin with.  The other problem I had with the game is how short it is.  I solved the entire game in two hours, which includes me leaving the game open while I made a sandwich.  I thought to myself "Oh.  It looks like I got about a third of the game done by now!" only to realize at that point, the entire game is only one chapter...  Oh well.  I still look forward to the next iterations.

title: The Journey Down: Chapter One

This can be confusing at times. But this is just nitpicking. The game is fun! And the music is simply great!

title: The Last Door - Collector's Edition
text: A simple but intriguing point and click. The Last Door is a pont and click adventure divided into 4 chapters. It's quite easy and I completed it without any hints in about 5 and a half hours. Most of the puzzles are intuitive, though there were times I followed the method of trying every inventory item on anything that is interactive in the game. The puzzles are mostly fun and progress the story very well. There are plenty of mini cut scenes to keep things flowing along. The story itself starts out very well and in the first couple of chapters it is very easy to follow, though by the third chapter I had pretty much lost track of what was going on and I was not clear what the ending was about. The ambient sounds in the game are done really well and the couple of jump scares are effective enough. The title musical score is a rousing piece and sets the tone of the game up very well. The characters themselves have no voiceovers, just silent text. My opinion on the graphics is mixed. I guess they managed to keep the budget down and thus be sure to put out a game. They are actually quite effective at times and add to the atmosphere and they help to make the puzzles more challenging as it's often not clear what you are looking at until you mouse over the hotspot and click it. Still, there were many times in the game when I was wishing for much clearer and detailed graphics as I was getting eye strain quite quickly at times. So generally I enjoyed this title and particularly appreciated the fair puzzles, being not too tough. I will purchase season 2 when it comes out and just hope the story is a little bit more coherent.

title: The Last Door - Collector's Edition
text: Depressing. This game is too depressing for me, the music sets the mood just fine. The graphics is a big turnoff for me, sure I get it pixel graphics! Let me tell you something about pixels, I grew up with pixel graphics, loved them on the 8-bit Nintendo and 16-bit Super Nintendo and Genesis, but pixel graphics are not meant for point & click games, especially in 2014 and beyond. I find it incredibly annoying requiring a magnifying glass to understand what the heck I'm looking at, seeing the objects to solve the puzzles is the whole concept of point & click games, so I find this game counterintuitive. Speaking of which I find the puzzles counterintuitive as well, who the heck grabs a dying crow then puts it in a cat bowl? Then goes looking for the cat that somehow magically hidden behind a wall which you require a hammer to break into. You could theorize the cat is a ghost, but then it shouldn't be able to scratch someone eyes out or eat the crow in the first place! Meh whatever the puzzles don't make any sense, but that's what type of game this is.

title: The Last Door - Collector's Edition
text: This game surprised me. I tend to chew through adventure games and spit most of them out in the process, looking for those rare gems and refusing to waste time with anything less. This one had me hooked right from the start. It hits those necessary notes perfectly and with careful deliberation. . Lots of games use pixel art to justify a low art budget, but this makes pixel art look pixelated. The resolution is something like 120x120, less than old CGA games. And as a result the art takes on this impressionistic feeling that just works in a compelling way. It's ultra low res, but it's crafted extremely well. The combination works in surprising ways. . The writing is good, and what isn't written is communicated visually with a similarly deft hand. . The orchestral soundtrack is absolutely bonkers in how good it is. A three hour long game should not have music this rich. . Finally, the length of the game is just right. It ends before any adventure game fatigue sets in. To be fair, if I had been waiting for this to come out episode-by-episode, I would have been less than impressed, but taken as a whole and burning through the entire game in a night, it fit. . It ends on a sequel which is a -1 point deduction, I can give them a pass. It still contains your typical adventure game inventory stuff, but I never really struggled with where to go or what to do next. The few instances where I did backtrack aimlessly were because I overlooked something clickable. That didn't happen often enough to frustrate me.
